title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A describing word copies the thing described: -aḥ for a man, -ā for a woman, -am for a neuter noun. dīrghaḥ, dīrghā and dīrgham are one word, and not one of them is the plain form the other two are built from.

mātāpitarau is ONE word meaning 'mother and father'. The two nouns are welded together and the ending on the end says 'two' — there is no word for 'and' anywhere inside it and no way to put one there.
Sanskrit counts in threes: one, TWO, and many. A pair takes endings of its own — mātāpitarau, vṛddhau, staḥ — and that is not a plural spelt differently.
The pair marking runs through the whole sentence. mama mātāpitarau vṛddhau has a dual noun and a dual adjective; add the verb and staḥ makes three agreements inside four words.
staḥ is 'the two are'. It is M3's asti carrying a dual ending, and it is the ONLY dual verb this course writes — no other verb is put in the dual anywhere in this level.
English adjectives never change at all. Sanskrit's always do, and they copy the NOUN's grammar rather than the person's sex: mitram is a neuter word, so a friend of either sex is mama mitram dīrgham.

mātā, pitā and bhrātā do not look like the nouns M1 taught, because they belong to a different stem class. Learn each as it stands; this course bends none of them, and the only bent shape it writes is the compound mātāpitarau.

A sentence about a relative needs no verb at all. mama bhaginī dīrghā is a possessive, a noun and an adjective, and it is complete — the present 'is' has been optional since M1. A sentence about WHERE somebody is still needs asti or staḥ.
A relationship noun carries the person's gender in the word itself — bhrātā against bhaginī, bālaḥ against bālā — so there is no single word covering both the way English 'sibling' does.

vṛddhaḥ is 'old' said of a PERSON, and it leans respectful rather than rude. It is not the word for an old object, so do not stretch it across both the way English 'old' stretches; describing people here stays with height, age and temperament.

words.note: 'I', here as mama, 'of me'. A relationship is said with the 'of' shape and nothing else — there is no separate word for 'my'.
'Mother'. It ends in -ā and is feminine, which is a coincidence rather than a rule — the next word, pitā, ends the same way and is a man.
'Calm': śāntaḥ of a man, śāntā of a woman, śāntam of a neuter noun, śāntau of a pair. One word, four shapes, chosen by what it describes.

sentences.trap: There is no word for 'is'. A possessive, a noun and an adjective stand side by side and that is the whole sentence, exactly as it was in M1.
sentences.sound: MA-ma MAA-taa SHAAN-taa. Three long ā's once the first word is past — hold every one. The ś of śāntā is the flat 'sh' of 'ship', and the n before the t is dental, tongue against the teeth.

variations.changed: the person described is a man, so the adjective moves to -aḥ and nothing else in the line moves
the adjective gives way to a noun, and the sentence is still verbless — two words side by side already say 'is'
a place enters, and with it M3's asti — a sentence about where somebody is does not drop its verb

mistake.why: The adjective has stayed masculine while the noun beside it is feminine. A Sanskrit adjective copies its noun every single time; there is no default shape that can be left alone.

sentences.usage: How you would describe your own family to somebody who has just met you.
sentences.mnemonic: mātā, with 'maternal' standing right behind it.

words.note: 'Father', and it is masculine although it ends in -ā. The ending on this noun says nothing about gender; the adjective beside it does.
'Old', said of a person and leaning respectful: vṛddhaḥ of a man, vṛddhā of a woman, vṛddhau of a pair. It is not the word for an old object.
'I' in its 'of me' shape, mama. It does not change for the gender of what follows it — only the adjective at the end does.

sentences.trap: pitā ends in -ā and is a MAN. Nothing about the shape of a noun in this class predicts its gender; you learn the gender with the word.
sentences.sound: MA-ma pi-TAA VRID-dhaḥ. The ddh of vṛddhaḥ is a doubled d with breath on the release — hold the first, then let the second out. The ṛ is the curled-back vowel, a short 'ri'.

variations.changed: the parent described is the mother, so the adjective goes to -ā — and nothing else does
a noun takes the adjective's place and the sentence stays verbless

variations.display: mama pitā vṛddhaḥ, tathāpi saḥ pratidinam paṭhati.
variations.script: मम पिता वृद्धः, तथापि सः प्रतिदिनम् पठति।
variations.cue: My father is old, even so he reads every day.
variations.changed: a second clause is hung on with M10's tathāpi, and saḥ picks up the father the first clause named

mistake.why: The adjective has been made feminine because pitā ends in -ā. It is the noun's gender that decides, not the noun's last letter, and pitā is masculine however it looks.

sentences.usage: Said with respect. Of a person vṛddhaḥ is nearer 'elder' than 'old'.
sentences.mnemonic: pitā, with 'paternal' standing right behind it.

words.note: 'Mother and father' in ONE word: the two nouns are welded and the -au on the end says 'two'. No word for 'and' is inside it, and it cannot be split.
'Old', here as vṛddhau because what it describes is a pair. The adjective takes the same -au the noun took.
'Of me', unchanged by the pair behind it. Only the noun and the adjective count; the possessive never does.

sentences.trap: There is no word for 'and' inside mātāpitarau and no way to put one there. The two nouns are welded, and the ending on the end is what says 'two'.
sentences.sound: MA-ma maa-taa-pi-ta-RAU VRID-dhau. One word, five syllables, no break in the middle — the joint between mātā and pitṛ is inside it and is never heard as a seam. The -au is the 'ow' of 'now'.

variations.changed: the adjective changes and keeps the dual ending — the pair marking sits on every word that describes them
a verb is added and it is dual too, which is the third agreement the pair demands
one person instead of a pair, so the noun and the adjective both fall back to the singular

mistake.why: The adjective has been made plural. Two is not 'many' in this language: a pair has its own ending, -au, and the adjective has to take the one the noun took.

sentences.usage: The ordinary way to speak of your parents as a pair; two separate sentences would sound like two separate subjects.
sentences.mnemonic: Mother-father-two. The count rides on the end of the pair, not on either half of it.

words.note: 'Mother and father', one word and one pair. Everything after it in the sentence has to agree with the two, including the verb.
M6's house in its 'at' shape, gṛhe. The -e is the whole of 'at home'; nothing stands in front of it.
'The two are' — M3's asti with a dual ending. It is the only dual verb this course writes: asti for one, staḥ for two.

sentences.trap: staḥ is not a plural asti. It is the shape for exactly two, and using it of three people would be as wrong as using asti of two.
sentences.sound: MA-ma maa-taa-pi-ta-RAU GRI-he STAḤ. staḥ is one syllable with st- together at the front. The e of gṛhe is long, as every e in this language is.

variations.cue: My parents are at the school.
variations.changed: the place changes and keeps its -e ending, which is what 'at' is made of
one person instead of two, so the dual staḥ falls back to M3's asti

variations.cue: My parents are not at home.
variations.changed: na negates the line and stands in front of the verb, exactly where M3 put it

mistake.why: asti is the shape for one. The pair has been marked on the noun and then forgotten on the verb — the half-agreement English never has to think about. Here the count is carried by every word that can carry it.

sentences.usage: The answer to 'where are your parents?' — the commonest sentence this module builds.
sentences.mnemonic: asti for one, staḥ for two. The verb counts as well.

words.note: 'Sister', the everyday word. It names a woman in the word itself, so no adjective beside it is ever masculine.
'Tall' of a person and 'long' of a thing — one word for both. dīrghaḥ of a man, dīrghā of a woman, dīrgham of a neuter noun.
'Of me'. The same mama has now stood in front of a mother, a father, a pair and a sister without changing once.

sentences.trap: dīrghā is 'tall' of a person and 'long' of a thing, and the same word does both. English needs two adjectives here; Sanskrit needs one.
sentences.sound: MA-ma bha-gi-NII DIIR-ghaa. The bh of bhaginī is a b with breath behind it, one sound and not two. Both ī's are long, and the r of dīrghā is a light tap before the gh.

variations.changed: the sibling is a brother, so the noun and the adjective change together
a name takes the adjective's place, and the sentence is two nouns with nothing between them

variations.cue: My sister is a student. She is tall.
variations.changed: the description moves into a second sentence, where sā picks up the sister without naming her again

mistake.why: The masculine ending has been left on an adjective describing a woman. bhaginī is feminine and the adjective has to follow it to dīrghā; there is no neutral shape to fall back on.

sentences.usage: Height, age and temperament are what this module describes people with.
sentences.mnemonic: dīrghā is 'long'. A tall person is a long one.

sentences.cue: My brother is a student. He is tall.

words.note: 'Brother', and it is the same word as English 'brother', five thousand years apart. Like mātā and pitā it ends in -ā and is never bent in this course.
M5's 'he', carrying the brother into the second sentence. Nothing joins the two sentences but this word.
'Tall', masculine here because saḥ is. The adjective agrees with the word in front of it, not with the noun two sentences back.

sentences.trap: saḥ is doing the work of English 'he', and it is the only thing holding the two sentences together — there is no conjunction of any kind between them.
sentences.sound: MA-ma BHRAA-taa CHAA-traḥ. SAḤ DIIR-ghaḥ. bhr- is one cluster, the bh breathed with the r tapped straight after it. Both sentences end in that breathed -aḥ, an echo of the a in front of it.

variations.cue: My sister is a student. She is tall.
variations.changed: every word that can carry gender changes at once — the noun, the pronoun and the adjective

variations.display: mama bhrātā chātraḥ. saḥ vidyālaye asti.
variations.script: मम भ्राता छात्रः। सः विद्यालये अस्ति।
variations.cue: My brother is a student. He is at the school.
variations.changed: the second sentence says where instead of what, so it needs asti where the first needed nothing

variations.display: mama bhrātā chātraḥ. saḥ pratidinam paṭhati.
variations.script: मम भ्राता छात्रः। सः प्रतिदिनम् पठति।
variations.cue: My brother is a student. He reads every day.
variations.changed: the second sentence takes a real verb, and saḥ is still what carries the brother into it

mistake.why: chātrā is the shape for a female student, and the brother has been given it. A noun naming a person carries that person's gender — M1's first lesson, and it does not stop applying because a relationship word stands in front of it.

sentences.usage: How you introduce a family member and then say one thing about them.
sentences.mnemonic: bhrātā and 'brother' are the same word, a very long time apart.

words.note: 'Friend', and the word is NEUTER. It does not change for who the friend is, and neither does the adjective beside it: mama mitram dīrgham, of a man or of a woman.
'Tall' in its neuter shape, dīrgham, because mitram is neuter. The ending reports the noun's grammar, not the person's sex.
'Of me'. Unchanged again — the possessive is the one word in these sentences that never agrees with anything.

sentences.trap: mitram is a NEUTER noun, so its adjective is neuter — dīrgham — whether the friend is a man or a woman. The ending reports the word's grammar, not the person.
sentences.sound: MA-ma MIT-ram DIIR-gham. Both words end in that -am, which is really a light m; said at speed it becomes a hum into the next word, and the page keeps the m.

variations.changed: a different adjective, and it takes the same neuter ending — the noun decides, every time
a place and a verb enter, and mitram does not change at all, because 'at home' is carried by the -e on the house
a woman is named as the friend and mitram stays neuter — the clearest proof that the word's gender is not the person's

mistake.why: The adjective has been made masculine because the friend is a man. It agrees with mitram, which is neuter, and nothing about the person outside the sentence can reach in and change it.

sentences.usage: The everyday word for a friend, and it never changes shape for who the friend is.
sentences.mnemonic: The language files a friend as neuter. Read nothing into it.

words.note: 'Boy', the masculine partner of M9's bālā, 'girl'. Neither is built from the other; each carries its own gender and its own ending.
M5's word, here as 'that' in front of a noun rather than 'he' standing alone. It agrees with the noun it points at.
'Calm', masculine to match the boy. Three words in a row ending -aḥ is not a rhyme; it is agreement.

sentences.trap: bālaḥ is the boy to M9's bālā, the girl — one word with two genders, and neither is made out of the other.
sentences.sound: SAḤ BAA-laḥ SHAAN-taḥ. Three words ending in the breathed -aḥ, each an echo of the vowel in front of it. The long ā of bālaḥ is the whole difference between it and a short one.

variations.changed: every word in the line changes gender together — the pronoun, the noun and the adjective

variations.cue: That boy is at the school.
variations.changed: the adjective gives way to a place, and a place needs asti where an adjective needed nothing
the adjective gives way to a second noun, and the sentence is still verbless

mistake.why: bālā is the girl. The masculine saḥ and the masculine śāntaḥ are both right and the noun between them has been left feminine — the one thing in the line that context cannot repair.

sentences.usage: Said about a child who is not in the conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: bālaḥ and bālā: the boy and the girl, one letter apart.

sentences.cue: Where are your parents? (to a man)

words.note: M2's polite 'you' in its 'of you' shape: bhavataḥ to a man, bhavatyāḥ to a woman. It does not change for the pair behind it.
M2's 'where', at the front of what it asks about. The question is marked by this word alone — nothing else in the line moves.
'The two are', in a question exactly as in a statement. A question does not suspend agreement: the pair is still a pair.

sentences.trap: bhavataḥ is 'of your honour' — the polite 'your'. It does not change for the pair behind it; only the noun and the verb do.
sentences.sound: bha-va-TAḤ maa-taa-pi-ta-RAU KU-tra STAḤ. kutra is a light tap of an r between two short vowels. The voice usually rises at the end, but kutra is what makes it a question.

variations.cue: Where are your parents? (to a woman)
variations.changed: the polite 'your' takes its feminine shape bhavatyāḥ, and nothing else in the question moves
one parent instead of two, so the noun and the verb both fall back to the singular
the answer, with kutra replaced by the place it was asking for and bhavataḥ by mama

mistake.why: The verb has been dropped, on the pattern of M2's bhavataḥ nāma kim? A sentence that says WHERE somebody is keeps its verb; only a sentence linking two nouns may go without one.

sentences.usage: The commonest polite question about somebody's family.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask with kutra, answer with staḥ. The pair stays dual on both sides.

sentences.display: mama bhrātā bhaginī ca vidyālaye staḥ.
sentences.script: मम भ्राता भगिनी च विद्यालये स्तः।
sentences.cue: My brother and sister are at the school.
sentences.literal: of-me brother sister and in-school are-two

words.note: 'Brother', first of the two joined by ca. Neither noun changes for being joined; only the verb at the end registers that there are two of them.
M10's 'and', standing after the last of the things it joins rather than between them. Two people joined by ca are still two.
'The two are'. A pair built with ca takes the same verb a welded compound would — the verb counts people, not words.

sentences.trap: Two nouns joined with ca still count as two, so the verb is staḥ. A pair made with ca and a pair welded into a compound behave identically once the verb is reached.
sentences.sound: MA-ma BHRAA-taa bha-gi-NII cha vi-dyaa-LA-ye STAḤ. ca is a single light syllable that leans on the word in front of it — bhaginii-cha, said as one.

variations.display: mama mātā pitā ca gṛhe staḥ.
variations.script: मम माता पिता च गृहे स्तः।
variations.cue: My mother and father are at home.
variations.changed: the pair is built with ca instead of the compound, and the verb is staḥ either way

variations.cue: My brother is at the school.
variations.changed: one person, so ca goes and the verb falls back to asti

variations.display: mama bhrātā bhaginī ca gṛhe staḥ.
variations.script: मम भ्राता भगिनी च गृहे स्तः।
variations.cue: My brother and sister are at home.
variations.changed: the place changes and keeps its -e, which is the only thing marking 'at'

mistake.display: mama bhrātā bhaginī ca vidyālaye asti.
mistake.why: ca has joined two people and the verb has stayed singular, as it might in English when the subject 'looks' single. Sanskrit counts what is actually there: two, so staḥ.

sentences.usage: Where a compound is not available, ca does the same job and the verb does not notice the difference.
sentences.mnemonic: Two people, however you joined them, take staḥ.

comprehensionPool.cue: My father is at the school.

comprehensionPool.display: mama bhaginī bhrātā ca gṛhe staḥ.
comprehensionPool.script: मम भगिनी भ्राता च गृहे स्तः।
comprehensionPool.cue: My sister and brother are at home.

comprehensionPool.display: mama pitā vṛddhaḥ. saḥ pratidinam paṭhati.
comprehensionPool.script: मम पिता वृद्धः। सः प्रतिदिनम् पठति।
comprehensionPool.cue: My father is old. He reads every day.

comprehensionPool.display: mama mātā śāntā, ataḥ aham api śāntaḥ.
comprehensionPool.script: मम माता शान्ता, अतः अहम् अपि शान्तः।
comprehensionPool.cue: My mother is calm, so I am calm too.
Sītā is my friend. She is a student.
